Paginated orderBy on a to-one relation uses the wrong alias when another populated relation has a same-named json property
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Ordering a paginated query by a to-one relation picks the wrong table alias as soon as another, **populated**, to-one relation has a property of the same name typed as `json`.

Filtering on a M:N relation makes the query return duplicate rows, so `limit` makes MikroORM select the ids in a grouped sub-query first. The `orderBy` term is wrapped in `MIN()` for that sub-query, and there the alias comes from the populated relation instead of the one named in `orderBy`. The two `ORDER BY` clauses of the same query end up naming different columns:

**The property must be `json` for this to happen.** With a plain string column on both relations the alias stays correct, which is what made this hard to narrow down.

### Two symptoms

On **SQLite** nothing fails: `MIN()` accepts the mismatched column, the sub-query keeps the wrong row, and the caller silently gets a different page than it asked for.

On **PostgreSQL** the query does not run at all, because the mismatched column is `jsonb`:

```
DriverException: function min(jsonb) does not exist
 - hint: No function matches the given name and argument types. You might need to add explicit type casts.
```

That is how we found it — a working GraphQL endpoint started returning a 500 after a routine patch update.

### Affected versions

| Version | Sub-query `ORDER BY` | SQLite | PostgreSQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1.5 | correct alias | ok | ok |
| 7.1.6 | wrong alias | wrong page, silent | `function min(jsonb) does not exist` |
| 7.2.1 | wrong alias | wrong page, silent | `function min(jsonb) does not exist` |

First bad version is **7.1.6**. The only change in that release touching this path is *"sql: support orderBy on persist(false) virtual fields with pagination"* (#7979).

### Reproduction

https://github.com/laurentmalgras/mikro-orm-reproduction/tree/orderby-alias-lost-in-pagination-subquery

`npm test` — `src/orderby-alias-pagination.test.ts` fails. In-memory SQLite, four entities, no external database needed.

`Task` has two to-one relations, `questionnaire` (json `name`) and `contributingEntity` (string `name`), plus a M:N `assignedContributors`:

```ts
await orm.em.find(
  Task,
  { assignedContributors: { id: { $in: [contributor.id] } } },
  {
    limit: 1,
    orderBy: { contributingEntity: { name: 'ASC' } },
    populate: ['questionnaire'],
  },
);
```

The emitted SQL, where `q1` is `questionnaire` and `c3` is `contributingEntity`:

```sql
-- sub-query
... group by `t0`.`id` order by min(`q1`.`name`) asc limit 1
-- outer query
... order by `c3`.`name` asc
```

The two fixtures are seeded so the orderings disagree: by `contributingEntity.name` taskA comes first, by `questionnaire.name` taskB does. The test asserts the cause and the consequence separately, so the failure names the defect directly:

```
AssertionError: expected 'q1' to be 'c3'
```

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

7.1.14 (first bad: 7.1.6, last good: 7.1.5)

### Node.js version

Node.js v24.11.0, TypeScript 5.9.3

### Operating system

_No response_

TPT: parent-table columns unreachable through a relation targeting a sub-class
items.body:
Hey @B4nan fast fix yesterday, thanks!! Another TPT bug below, similar to the last one there's a couple ways to go about it so filing an issue rather than PR.

Two defects when an `m:1` targets a **TPT sub-class**: a column on a parent table cannot be reached
through the relation. Verified on sqlite, PostgreSQL 16 and MSSQL 2025.

```ts
@Filter({ name: 'softDelete', cond: { deletedAt: null }, default: true })   // only needed for defect 2
@Entity({ inheritance: 'tpt' })
class Animal {
  @PrimaryKey() id!: number;
  @Property() name!: string;
  @Property({ nullable: true }) deletedAt?: Date;
}

@Entity()
class Dog extends Animal {
  @Property() breed!: string;
}

@Entity()
class Tag {
  @PrimaryKey() id!: number;
  @ManyToOne(() => Dog) dog!: Dog;   // must be non-nullable for defect 2
}
```

## Defect 1 — `where`/`orderBy` on an inherited property never joins the parent table

```ts
await em.find(Tag, { dog: { name: 'Rex' } }, { filters: false });
```
```sql
from `tag` as `t0` inner join `dog` as `d1` on `t0`.`dog_id` = `d1`.`id`
where `d1`.`name` = 'Rex'          -- `animal` is never joined
```
`no such column: d1.name` / `column d1.name does not exist` / `Invalid column name 'name'`.

Also affects `orderBy`, `count`, `$in`, `groupBy` and `qb.joinAndSelect()`. Adding
`populate: ['dog'], strategy: 'joined'` to the query above makes it pass — populating adds the join
the criteria path does not. In a 3-level hierarchy it is any column not on the leaf table, not just
the root's: `where { puppy: { breed } }` fails too.

**Cause.** `applyTPTJoins()` walks the parent chain of `this.mainAlias.meta` only.
`AbstractSqlDriver.addTPTParentJoinsForRelation()` does the right walk for a relation target, but is
only reachable from `getFieldsForJoinedLoad()`, i.e. the joined-populate path. The criteria auto-join
(`ObjectCriteriaNode` → `joinReference()`) never calls it.

## Defect 2 — a filter condition on an inherited column forward-references the parent join

Needs the relation to be **non-nullable** — nullable gives a `leftJoin`, which `processNestedJoins()`
nests for unrelated reasons, incidentally bringing the alias into scope.

```ts
await em.find(Tag, {});
```
```sql
from `tag` as `t0`
inner join `dog` as `d1` on `t0`.`dog_id` = `d1`.`id` and `a2`.`deleted_at` is null  -- a2 not in scope
inner join `animal` as `a2` on `d1`.`id` = `a2`.`id`
```
`missing FROM-clause entry for table "a2"` / `The multi-part identifier "a2.deleted_at" could not be
bound.` sqlite silently accepts it, which is presumably why the sqlite TPT suite does not catch it.

**Cause.** `mergeOnConditions()` attaches the condition to the join whose alias prefixes the key
(`d1.deletedAt`), but `getTPTAliasForProperty()` re-qualifies it to `a2` at render time.
`nestReferencedJoins()` guards against exactly this, but `condReferencesAlias()` is a literal
`startsWith`, so it never fires for an inherited column — and `mergeOnConditions()` does not call it
at all.

## Related, not addressed

- `#state.tptAlias` uses two keying schemes (bare `className` vs `leafAlias:className`); I could not
  make them collide, flagging as a latent trap only.
- Defect 2 is invisible on sqlite, so a regression test needs postgres/mssql or an SQL assertion.

I have a fix for both (~30 lines in `packages/sql`), green with no regressions — happy to PR. One
design fork if you want it: I nest the parent join into the sub-class join group, but attaching the
condition to the parent join's own `on` would be flatter. It also drops `protected` from
`addTPTParentJoinsForRelation()`, which you may want at a different seam.

## Reproduction

https://github.com/Subtletree/mikro-orm/tree/repro/tpt-relation-to-subtype

One commit on master (35092380a), one test file, no source changes.
`yarn test tpt-relation-to-subtype` → 6 failing, 3 passing. The 3 are controls (same relation reaching
a sub-class-owned property; reading the sub-class directly by an inherited property), so the failures
are attributable to going through the relation rather than to TPT generally.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| MikroORM version | master @ `35092380a` (unreleased; 7.1.14 is the latest published and predates #8227 / #8228 / #8229) |
| Driver | `@mikro-orm/sqlite`, `@mikro-orm/postgresql`, `@mikro-orm/mssql` |
| Node.js | 22.20.0 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2) |

items.title: applyJoinedFilters() never terminates when entity filters form a relation cycle
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`QueryBuilder.applyJoinedFilters()` iterates `this.#state.autoJoinedPaths` with `for…of`, while `CriteriaNode.process()` — called inside that loop — pushes new paths onto the same array via `qb.scheduleFilterCheck()`. Array iterators are live, so the loop visits what it just appended.

When two entity filters reference each other through relations, this never terminates. Each lap schedules the next lap's joins and the criteria-node graph doubles, until the process dies with `JavaScript heap out of memory`. No error, no cycle detection, no depth cap.

Works in v6.6.14, fails in v7.1.14.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/jonasnilsberg/mikro-orm-filter-cycle-repro

```
npm install && node --max-old-space-size=256 repro.mjs   # 7.1.14 -> OOM
cd v6-control && npm install && node repro.mjs           # 6.6.14 -> ok
```

The heap cap only makes it fail fast; it OOMs at any size.

Three entities, two filters that traverse relations and close a cycle
(`ManagementObject → deviations → DeviationType → deviations → managementObject → …`):

```js
// ManagementObject
auth: { cond: ({ company }) => ({
  $or: [{ company }, { deviations: { type: { identifier: company } } }] }), default: true }

// DeviationType
auth: { cond: ({ company }) => ({ deviations: { managementObject: { company } } }), default: true }
```

```js
await em.find(ManagementObject, { deviations: { type: { identifier: "x" } } });
```

Both filters must traverse relations — one relational plus one scalar terminates fine.

### Actual

Instrumenting the loop shows `autoJoinedPaths` growing in lockstep with the iteration index:

```
iter=5  len=8   DeviationType.deviations
iter=6  len=8   DeviationType.deviations.managementObject
iter=7  len=10  DeviationType.deviations          <- cycle
iter=75 len=78  ...
FATAL ERROR: heap out of memory
```

A heap snapshot at the limit holds 131,073 (2^17 + 1) `ObjectCriteriaNode` instances, consistent with doubling once per cycle.

### Expected

The query completes, or MikroORM throws a descriptive error about the cyclic filter graph.

### Root cause

v6 stripped nested conditions from a relation-level filter and skipped the join when nothing scalar remained:

```js
if (!Utils.hasObjectKeys(cond)) continue;
```

A purely-nested filter was therefore discarded, so no cycle could form. v7 dropped that early exit and moved a `process()` call in front of the stripping:

```js
const criteriaNode = CriteriaNodeFactory.createNode(this.metadata, join.prop.targetMeta.class, cond);
cond = criteriaNode.process(this, { matchPopulateJoins: true, filter: true, … });
```

Resolving nested filter conditions into real joins looks like a deliberate improvement over v6 silently dropping them — the problem is only that the new traversal has no termination condition.

That same removed early exit also causes #8210, where a nested filter path binds to a join alias from a sibling branch. Two failure modes, one origin: cyclic filter graphs run away here, duplicated relations misresolve there.

### Versions

| Dependency | Version |
| ---------- | ------- |
| node | 22.23.1 |
| mikro-orm | 7.1.14 (fails; also 7.1.11, 7.1.12) / 6.6.14 (works) |
| your-driver | `@mikro-orm/sqlite` (code path is in `@mikro-orm/sql`, so all SQL drivers) |

items.title: Relation filter binds to a sibling branch's join alias, producing a forward alias reference
items.body:
### Describe the bug

When two default filters on an entity each traverse the same to-many relation, it gets auto-joined twice, in two branches. A filter on the *target* entity is merged into the `on` clause of both joins — but a nested relation path inside that filter resolves to a join created under the *other* branch. That alias renders later, so the query is rejected:

```
sqlite:   ON clause references tables to its right
postgres: missing FROM-clause entry for table "u3"
```

Works in v6.6.16, fails in v7.1.14.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/jonasnilsberg/mikro-orm-v7-sibling-branch-alias

```
npm install && node repro.mjs                    # 7.1.14 -> throws
cd v6-control && npm install && node repro.mjs   # 6.6.16 -> ok
```

`Mobile 1--* ManagementObject *--1 User *--1 Location`. Two filters on `Mobile` — one scalar-only (`managementObjects.status`), one traversing `managementObjects.user.location` — plus a `{ user: { location: 1 } }` filter on `ManagementObject`. Then `em.find(Mobile, {})`.

### Actual

```sql
select m0.* from mobile m0
left join management_object m1
  on m0.id = m1.mobile_id and u3.location_id = ?          -- u3 not in scope yet
left join (management_object m2 left join user u3 on m2.user_id = u3.id)
  on m0.id = m2.mobile_id and u3.location_id = ?
where m1.status in (?, ?) and u3.location_id = ?
```

`u3` belongs to m2's branch, so m1's `on` clause is both invalid SQL and pointing at the wrong row.

### Expected

m1 resolves `user` to its own join:

```sql
left join (management_object m1 left join user u4 on m1.user_id = u4.id)
  on m0.id = m1.mobile_id and u4.location_id = ?
```

### Root cause

`applyJoinedFilters()` processes the filter with `ignoreBranching: true`, so `getJoinForPath()` strips `[\d+]` and matches across branches:

```
want = Mobile[0].managementObjects.user  ->  u3 @ Mobile[1].managementObjects.user
```

`nestReferencedJoins()` (added for #7681, #8090, #8099) would normally fold a referenced join into the `on` clause, but it only scans the join's own subtree — and `u3`'s owner is `m2`. Folding wouldn't be right here anyway; m1 needs its own join.

The same removed early exit in `applyJoinedFilters()` also causes #8211, where a cyclic filter graph expands until the process runs out of memory. Two failure modes, one origin.

Skipping candidates whose branch markers conflict, in the two branch-insensitive lookups in `getJoinForPath()`, produces the expected SQL. Happy to open a PR if that's the direction you'd take.

### Versions

| Dependency | Version |
| ---------- | ------- |
| node | 22.23.1 |
| mikro-orm | 7.1.14 (fails) / 6.6.16 (works) |
| your-driver | `@mikro-orm/sqlite` |

items.title: Key every user-class lookup by class reference, not class name (follow-up to #8107)
items.body:
Follow-up to #8107.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

#8107 asked for the decorator metadata registry to be keyed by class reference "end to end". The fix that landed covers discovery, and it works: `MetadataStorage.getMetadata` keys by `META_SYMBOL`, `initRelation` resolves through `prop.target` before falling back to a name, and a 166-entity schema discovers cleanly under a bundler that mangles every class name.

The assumption that a class name identifies a class survives everywhere around discovery, and those paths are the ones that fail now. Each one costs a production debugging session to find, and several of the remaining ones fail silently rather than throwing.

How bad the collisions are, in a Next.js 16 Turbopack server build: in one chunk, 129 entity classes occupy 17 distinct minified names. One name, `d`, is shared by 19 entities. All six user-defined `Type` subclasses minify to `a`. Collisions are the default under this bundler, not an edge case.

One relevant detail: MikroORM resolves as an external and ships unminified, so its own classes keep their names. Only **user-supplied** classes get mangled. That scopes the problem — every lookup that keys a user class by name is affected, and nothing internal to the library is.

The confirmed failure is in `EventManager`, which dispatches entity events by name:

```js
// events/EventManager.js:87
return new Set(
  listener.getSubscribedEntities().map((name) => Utils.className(name)),
);

// events/EventManager.js:46
if (entities.size === 0 || !entity || entities.has(entity.constructor.name)) {
  listeners.push(listener[event].bind(listener));
}
```

A subscriber declaring `getSubscribedEntities() { return [Foo] }` received `beforeCreate` for an unrelated entity that mangled to the same name, and crashed reading a relation that entity does not have:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')
     at Object.beforeCreate
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

An audit of every lookup that resolves a user-supplied class, keying each by class reference or `_id` the way discovery now does, rather than another point fix.

Line numbers are from 7.1.14-dev.10. Only the first row is confirmed by a stack trace; the rest come from reading the source, and I have not built a reproduction for each.

| Location                                                                 | Key                                 | Consequence of a collision                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `events/EventManager.js:46,87`                                           | `entity.constructor.name`           | Subscriber runs for a foreign entity. **Confirmed.**                                                                                                                                                             |
| `EntityManager.js:263` (`addFilter`)                                     | `Utils.className(entity)`           | A global filter registered for one entity applies to another. Silent, and a tenancy filter landing on the wrong entity is a data-exposure bug.                                                                   |
| `EntityManager.js:2119` (cache key)                                      | `Utils.className(entityName)`       | Result cache returns another entity's rows for the same method and query shape. Silent.                                                                                                                          |
| `types/Type.js:57` (`Type.getType`)                                      | `cls.name`                          | Returns a cached instance of a different `Type` subclass. Silent value corruption. Discovery uses `new prop.type()` so it is off that path today, but `getType` is public API.                                   |
| `metadata/MetadataStorage.js:91,102`                                     | `Utils.className`                   | `find()` falls back to the class-name map and `set()` writes it, so the last class registered under a shared name wins every name-based lookup.                                                                  |
| `entity/EntityRepository.js:225`                                         | both sides by name                  | `validateRepositoryType` compares two mangled names, so a wrong-entity call passes validation.                                                                                                                   |
| `metadata/MetadataDiscovery.js:2141`                                     | `Utils.className(cls)`              | `forceEntityConstructor: [A, B]` matches unrelated entities.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `metadata/MetadataDiscovery.js:234`, `metadata/MetadataValidator.js:116` | `prop.type` string vs `m.className` | The "entity not discovered" checks pass on a name match against the wrong entity. `MetadataDiscovery.js:228` already pairs its name check with `discoveredByIdentity`; these two did not get the same treatment. |

Where a name is genuinely load-bearing — STI, `discriminatorMap`, `EntitySchema` string names, `em.find('Foo', …)` — keeping it is fine, documented as requiring stable class names. The distinction I would suggest: a class name is fine for producing a message, and never fine for deciding which class something is.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Dropping `getSubscribedEntities()` and narrowing with `instanceof` inside every hook. This works, but it means the documented filtering API cannot be used at all on a minifying bundler.
- Bundler-side `keep_classnames`, requested in vercel/next.js#96574. Next implemented turbopack client only minification configuration in upcoming 16.4 (vercel/next.js#96578)
- `EntitySchema` with explicit names, as #8107 noted, means abandoning the decorator API across the app.

**Additional context**

`@mikro-orm/core` 7.1.14-dev.10, `@mikro-orm/decorators` legacy decorators, `@mikro-orm/postgresql`, Next.js 16.3.3, Turbopack server build with minification on. Explicit `tableName` on all 166 entities, explicit entity arrays, explicit `type` on every property.

Four of these surfaced in a single migration to a minifying bundler: table-name derivation, `discriminatorMap` resolution, the metadata registry from #8107, and the event manager, with #8107's fix already in place for the last one. Happy to test a canary, and I can share the script that produces the collision census above if a reproduction fixture would help.

items.title: @mikro-orm/entity-generator: Single-column partial indexes are incorrectly filtered out and omitted
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hello,

When running the entity generator, partial indexes (indexes containing a `WHERE` clause) that apply to only a single column are silently dropped. Multi-column partial indexes are successfully recovered, making this edge case easy to miss.

**The Root Cause**
In `packages/sql/src/schema/DatabaseTable.ts`, there is a discrepancy between two conditions regarding whether `index.where` makes an index non-trivial:

```ts
// ~Line 299: The prefilter before the loop
index.deferMode || index.expression || …          // index.where is NOT considered

// ~Line 355: The isTrivial check inside the loop
!index.deferMode && !index.expression && !index.where && …   // index.where IS considered

```

Because the earlier prefilter omits `index.where`, a single-column partial index never makes it into the loop to be evaluated by the `isTrivial` check.

**Impact**
In many schemas, partial indexes are not just performance optimizations—they enforce critical data integrity rules. For example, this index guarantees one root node per tenant:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_org_nodes_tenant_single_root
  ON org_nodes (tenant_id) WHERE parent_id IS NULL;

```

Without it, a tenant could theoretically have multiple roots, breaking the tree structure without throwing an error at insertion time.

Similar to check constraints, the generator already has the correct fallback logic for objects it cannot map cleanly (falling back to a raw expression around line 376). The issue is purely that the prefilter prevents single-column partial indexes from ever reaching that logic.

### Reproduction

You can reproduce this by creating a table with two partial indexes: one single-column and one multi-column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE probe (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
  parent_id uuid
);

-- Single-column + WHERE: This will be dropped
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_probe_single_root ON probe (tenant_id) WHERE parent_id IS NULL;

-- Multi-column + WHERE: This is successfully recovered
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_probe_pair ON probe (tenant_id, parent_id) WHERE parent_id IS NOT NULL;

```

**Expected:** Both indexes are present in the generated entity declaration.
**Actual:** Only the multi-column index (`uq_probe_pair`) is generated; the single-column index is completely omitted.

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

7.1.10 (@mikro-orm/core, @mikro-orm/postgresql, @mikro-orm/sql)

### Node.js version

v24.18.0, TypeScript 6.0.3

### Operating system

macOS 27.0 (arm64)

items.title: applyJoinedFilters forward-references an alias created by an earlier joined path (errorMissingRTE)
items.body:
`QueryBuilder.applyJoinedFilters` applies a joined entity's own `@Filter` to its join's `ON` clause. When that filter references a relation whose alias was already created by an **earlier** joined path, the condition is emitted into an `ON` clause that references the alias **before** its join is added → `missing FROM-clause entry for table "l2"` on PostgreSQL.

Sibling of #8090; **not** fixed by #8091 (reproduces with it applied and unapplied). Independent of the `autoJoinRefsForFilters` setting (default, `true`, or `false`) — the joins here come from the filter conditions themselves, not from ref auto-joining.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/jonasnilsberg/mikro-orm-v7-nested-filter-forward-ref

```bash
pnpm install && createdb mikro_orm_v7_nested_filter_repro && pnpm test
```

Three entities, each with a `default: true` `@Filter` named `auth`:
- `Grant` → `User`: `{ user: { location: { company } } }`
- `User` → `Location`: `{ location: { company } }`
- `Location` → `Company`: `{ company }`

Query: `em.findOne(Grant, {}, { fields: ['id'] })`.

### Generated SQL (buggy)

```sql
select "g0"."id" from "grant" as "g0"
inner join "user" as "u1"
  on "g0"."user_id" = "u1"."id" and "l2"."company_id" = 1   -- ❌ l2 not yet defined
inner join "location" as "l2"
  on "u1"."location_id" = "l2"."id" and "l2"."company_id" = 1
where "l2"."company_id" = 1
```

The `Grant` filter builds the `user` (`u1`) and `location` (`l2`) joins. `applyJoinedFilters` then applies `User`'s own filter to the `u1` join, resolving to `l2.company` — and emits it into `u1`'s `ON`, referencing `l2`, which is only joined on the next line.

### Root cause

`applyJoinedFilters` has a fold (added in #8091 / #7681) that nests joins created **during the current join's pass** (`joinCountBefore …`) to avoid exactly this forward reference. But `l2` was created earlier by the `Grant` filter's path, so it's before `joinCountBefore` and the fold skips it.

### Expected

`l2` must be defined before any `ON` references it (order the `location` join first, or route the condition to `WHERE` as the `Grant` filter's equivalent already does).

### Versions

- `@mikro-orm/core` / `@mikro-orm/postgresql`: 7.1.7
- Node.js: 22.x · PostgreSQL: 14+

items.title: applyJoinedFilters with autoJoinRefsForFilters: false references a join alias before it is defined (errorMissingRTE)
items.body:
## Bug: `applyJoinedFilters` with `autoJoinRefsForFilters: false` references a join alias before it is defined (`errorMissingRTE`)

When `autoJoinRefsForFilters: false` is set and a query auto-joins an entity whose `@Filter` condition references a relation, the generated SQL references a table alias in a join ON clause **before** that alias is defined in the FROM clause, causing `missing FROM-clause entry for table "l2"` (`errorMissingRTE`).

### Reproduction

https://github.com/jonasnilsberg/mikro-orm-v7-applyjoinedfilters-bug

```bash
pnpm install
createdb mikro_orm_v7_bug_repro
pnpm test
```

### Setup

- `Product` has M:1 → `Company`
- `Company` has a `@Filter` with `{ $or: [{ id: company }, { locations: locations }] }` where `locations` is a O:M relation
- ORM config has `autoJoinRefsForFilters: false`
- Query: `em.find(Product, { company: { code: 'ACME' } }, { filters: { auth: true } })`

### Generated SQL (buggy)

```sql
select "p0".* from "product" as "p0"
inner join "company" as "c1" on "p0"."company_id" = "c1"."id"
  and ("c1"."id" in ('company-1') or "l2"."id" in ('loc-1'))  -- ❌ l2 not yet defined
left join "location" as "l2" on "c1"."id" = "l2"."company_id"  -- defined too late
where "c1"."code" = 'ACME'
```

The `l2` alias (Location, created by the filter's `{ locations: [...] }` condition) is referenced in the Company join ON clause, but the Location join is added **after** the Company join.

### Expected behavior

With `autoJoinRefsForFilters: false`, the filter's `{ locations: [...] }` leg (alias `l2`) should be emitted so that no join ON clause references an alias before it is defined in FROM — either by placing each leg in its own join's ON clause (as the `true` path does) or by ordering the `l2` join before the `c1` join that references it.

Note this is **not** a FROM-ordering difference between the two settings. With `autoJoinRefsForFilters: true` (default), `l2` is *still* emitted after `c1` in the FROM clause — the query works because the `true` path splits the filter's `$or` legs into each join's own ON clause, so the company join never forward-references `l2`:

```sql
inner join "company" as "c1" on "p0"."company_id" = "c1"."id"
  and "c1"."id" in ('company-1')                              -- ✅ no l2 ref
left join "location" as "l2" on "c1"."id" = "l2"."company_id"
  and "l2"."id" in ('loc-1')                                  -- l2 leg in its own ON
where "c1"."code" = 'ACME'
```

The `false` path instead collapses both legs into the `c1` join's ON clause as `("c1"."id" in (…) or "l2"."id" in (…))`, referencing `l2` before its `left join` is emitted → `errorMissingRTE`.

### Additional note (possible second issue)

The two settings don't appear semantically equivalent even when both produce valid SQL. `false` preserves a real disjunction `(c1.id = … OR l2.id = …)`, whereas `true` splits the legs across an INNER (`c1`) and a LEFT (`l2`) join — since the `l2` leg sits in a LEFT-join ON clause it doesn't filter rows, effectively reducing the `$or` to just the `c1.id` leg. This may be a separate correctness bug in how `$or` filter conditions spanning a to-many relation are lowered.

### Versions

- `@mikro-orm/core`: 7.1.7
- `@mikro-orm/postgresql`: 7.1.7
- Node.js: 22.x
- PostgreSQL: 14+

items.title: migration:up poisons snapshot with migration-owned external triggers
items.body:
### Describe the bug

`migrator.up()` rewrites the migration snapshot from live introspection. If a
migration creates a PostgreSQL trigger with custom SQL, that trigger is copied
into the entity-metadata snapshot even though it is not declared in entity
metadata.

The next `migrator.checkSchema()` returns `true` and `migration:check` asks for a
new migration that drops the trigger. This makes migration-owned PostgreSQL
artifacts and snapshots incompatible.

### Reproduction

Minimal pnpm-only reproduction:

https://gist.github.com/vkartaviy/3607e3da5111d8f659a50f84df6394f0

It uses one `EntitySchema` table and one external statement trigger. The script
creates and drops its own uniquely named PostgreSQL database.

```text
{
  "after": {
    "hash": "46488bed6cae2d389ac7a82ca7c8ffe31c214d36f83be406091862c76d5bfdb2",
    "triggerCount": 1
  },
  "before": {
    "hash": "42bc441236a7512dd41b9b78d738d9de835bf5201578a17f918f25db1d9794e5",
    "triggerCount": 0
  },
  "migrationNeeded": true
}
```

### Expected behavior

Migration-owned triggers that are absent from target entity metadata should
remain in the live database but should not be copied into the entity-metadata
snapshot. ORM-managed triggers declared through `EntitySchema.triggers` must
continue to round-trip normally.

### Additional context

The behavior comes from `Migrator.runMigrations()`: after `up`/`down`, it
introspects the live schema and compares/stores it without distinguishing
metadata-managed triggers from migration-owned external triggers.

A local proof-of-concept filters introspected triggers against
`schemaGenerator.getTargetSchema()` before snapshot comparison/storage. It
keeps the external-trigger snapshot byte-identical with
`checkSchema() === false`, while a separate `EntitySchema.triggers` control also
stays byte-identical and retains its managed trigger.

Versions used:

- MikroORM 7.1.8
- PostgreSQL 17.9
- Node.js 24.14.1
- pnpm 11.13.0

### Describe the bug

When running a schema update (schema:update or programmatically via orm.schema.update()) on an Oracle database, MikroORM fails to detect existing tables if the database user is different from the dbName specified in the connection configuration.

Because the existing schema metadata is not properly resolved or filtered under these conditions, the Schema Generator assumes the tables do not exist and generates redundant CREATE TABLE statements. items.title: TPT: base enum CHECK constraint duplicated onto child subtype tables
items.body:
### Describe the bug

For TPT entities with an enum on the base table, the generated schema duplicates the enum's CHECK constraint onto the child tables.

Below is a verbose AI description:

---

  With `inheritance: 'tpt'`, schema generation emits a **base** entity's enum `CHECK` constraint onto the **child** subtype table as well. In TPT the column lives only on the parent table, so the child-table CHECK references a non-existent column and the generated DDL is invalid — `schema.create()` / `migration:up` fails.

  - **sqlite:** `no such column: status`
  - **mssql:** error **207**, `Invalid column name 'status'`

  This is **driver-independent** — the wrong-table constraint is produced in the shared schema layer (`DatabaseSchema.fromMetadata`), so it reproduces on sqlite, mssql, postgres and mysql. The reproduction uses in-memory sqlite per the template guidance.

  ## Entities (defineEntity; same happens with the decorator API)

  ```ts
  enum Status { ACTIVE = 'active', INACTIVE = 'inactive' }

  const PersonSchema = defineEntity({
    name: 'Person', abstract: true, inheritance: 'tpt',
    properties: { id: p.integer().primary(), name: p.string(), status: p.enum(() => Status) },
  });
  class Person extends PersonSchema.class {}
  PersonSchema.setClass(Person);

  const EmployeeSchema = defineEntity({
    name: 'Employee', extends: PersonSchema,
    properties: { department: p.string() }, // no `status` here
  });
  class Employee extends EmployeeSchema.class {}
  EmployeeSchema.setClass(Employee);
  ```

  ## Expected

  The `status` CHECK is emitted on the `person` table only.

  ## Actual

  `getCreateSchemaSQL()` also emits a CHECK on `employee`, whose table has no `status` column:

  ```sql
  create table `person` (`id` integer not null primary key autoincrement, `name` text not null, `status` text check (`status` in ('active', 'inactive')) not null);
  create table `employee` (`department` text not null, `id` integer not null primary key, constraint `employee_id_foreign` foreign key (`id`) references `person` (`id`) on update cascade on delete cascade,
  constraint `employee_status_check` check (`status` in ('active', 'inactive')));
  -- the `employee` table has no `status` column
  ```

  `await orm.schema.create()` then throws `no such column: status`.

  ## Notes

 - The runtime persistence layer already handles this correctly — inserting an `Employee` writes `status` to `person` and only `department`/PK to `employee`.
  - It's only DDL generation that's wrong: `DatabaseSchema.fromMetadata` already restricts TPT child **columns** to `ownProps`, but the **checks** loop iterates `meta.checks` (including inherited entries) without that filter, so inherited enum CHECKs leak onto child tables.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/Subtletree/mikro-orm-tpt-check-repro

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/mssql

### MikroORM version

7.1.4 also tested on 7.1.5-dev.26

### Node.js version

22.20.0

Ubuntu

items.title: Lightweight entities or query results
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I'm using mikro-orm to render many paginated data grids. These are read-only and I don't work with the resulting entities, I just load them disabling the identity map and serialise them to JSON. And usually that's fine since we only show one page, perhaps 20-50 items. However we have an export feature that loads large pages (1000 items) and iterates through them. Here the time spent in mikro-orm far exceeds the query time (maybe 30:1). Obviously the QueryBuilder would avoid this problem but mikro-orm does a lot of heavy lifting in the find() and findByCursor() functions: resolving path expressions, joining the right tables, sorting by the cursor expressions and so on. So we cannot just drop using them in the generic case only perhaps in a few optimised cases.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would like to see a flag there the find and findByCursor or similar functions can output a lightweight result - basically the result of the query if a join-strategy worked. Or perhaps something mapped back to the properties. Or maybe more, anything that would skip the most expensive part of having full entities that are not really necessary in this case.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I have considered using the QueryBuilder but it's not a practical solution since we have many grids, highly flexible and would end up re-implementing much of what the entity query-layer already does.

items.title: Array `$contains` (`@>`) nested under a relation in `populateWhere` is serialized as a record tuple in the JOIN-ON condition
items.body:
### Describe the bug

After upgrading to v7, a **multi-element** array operator (`$contains` / `@>`) that lands inside a **JOIN-ON** predicate is serialized as a record tuple instead of an array literal. A condition lands in the JOIN-ON when it is **nested under a relation** — e.g. inside `populateWhere`, or a relation filter inside `where`.

Concretely, `{ scope: { $contains: ['DEAL', 'PROJECT'] } }` nested under a relation produces:

```sql
... inner join "tag" "t1" on "t0"."tag_id" = "t1"."id"
    and "t1"."scope" @> ('{DEAL,PROJECT}', undefined)
```

i.e. the array is collapsed into a 2-element **tuple** whose first element is the full array literal `'{DEAL,PROJECT}'` and whose second element is the literal `undefined`. Postgres then fails with:

```
column "undefined" does not exist
```

The **same filter placed in the flat top-level WHERE serializes correctly**:

```sql
... where "t0"."scope" @> '{DEAL,PROJECT}'   -- correct
```

A **single-element** array is harmless because `@> ('{DEAL}')` is equivalent to `@> '{DEAL}'`; the bug only manifests with **2+ elements**.

This is a regression from v6, where the array literal was produced in both positions.

> Note: depending on the exact column type / nesting, the malformed tuple can also surface as `operator does not exist: text[] @> record` (SQLSTATE 42883) instead of `column "undefined" does not exist`. Both stem from the same root cause: the array operand is rendered as a record/tuple in the JOIN-ON code path rather than as an array.

## Reproduction

Minimal runnable repro (entities + a 3-test vitest file) is here: **https://github.com/jison228/mikroorm-contains-joinon-repro**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jison228/mikroorm-contains-joinon-repro
cd mikroorm-contains-joinon-repro && npm install
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/your_db npm test
# -> middle test fails: column "undefined" does not exist
```

The essence:

```ts
@Entity()
class Tag {
  @PrimaryKey({ type: 'number' }) id!: number;

  @Enum({ items: () => Scope, array: true }) // also reproduces with @Property({ type: 'string[]' })
  scope!: Scope[];

  @OneToMany(() => Item, (i) => i.tag) items = new Collection<Item>(this);
}

@Entity()
class Item {
  @PrimaryKey({ type: 'number' }) id!: number;
  @ManyToOne(() => Tag) tag!: Tag;
}

// ✅ flat WHERE -> "scope" @> '{DEAL,PROJECT}'
await em.find(Tag, { scope: { $contains: ['DEAL', 'PROJECT'] } });

// ❌ same filter under a relation -> JOIN-ON -> "scope" @> ('{DEAL,PROJECT}', undefined)
await em.find(Item, {}, {
  populate: ['tag'],
  populateWhere: { tag: { scope: { $contains: ['DEAL', 'PROJECT'] } } },
});
```

Verified against PostgreSQL with both an `@Enum({ items, array: true })` column and a plain `@Property({ type: 'string[]' })` column — identical malformed JOIN-ON output in both cases.

## Expected behavior

The array operator should serialize identically whether the predicate lands in the flat WHERE or in a JOIN-ON condition — always as an array literal / single array-bound parameter (`"scope" @> '{DEAL,PROJECT}'`), never as a record tuple `("...", undefined)`.

## Additional context

- This looks like the same class of bug as a previously reported/fixed JOIN-ON array case, but reached via `populateWhere` on a relation; the array-vs-tuple handling does not appear to be applied in this JOIN-ON path.
- Single-element arrays mask the bug (`(?)` === `?`); reproduce with **2+** elements.

items.body:
### Describe the bug

_See repro_: https://github.com/stoneLeaf/mikro-orm-v7-repros/tree/tpt-base-filter-breaks-eager-onetoone-population

### Context

Abstract TPT base entity with a soft-delete filter, a "part" entity with inverse OneToOne relations back to two concrete subtypes, and those subtypes each holding an eager owner-side OneToOne to the part entity:

```TypeScript
const PersonSchema = defineEntity({
  name: "Person",
  abstract: true,
  inheritance: "tpt",
  filters: {
    excludeDeleted: { name: "excludeDeleted", cond: { deletedAt: null }, default: true },
  },
  properties: {
    id: p.integer().primary(),
    name: p.string(),
    deletedAt: p.datetime().nullable(),
  },
});

const BadgeSchema = defineEntity({
  name: "Badge",
  properties: {
    id: p.integer().primary(),
    code: p.string(),
    parentEmployee: () => p.oneToOne(Employee).mappedBy("badge").ref().nullable(),
    parentContractor: () => p.oneToOne(Contractor).mappedBy("temporaryBadge").ref().nullable(),
  },
});

// Concrete subtype with an eager owner-side OneToOne to Badge
const EmployeeSchema = defineEntity({
  name: "Employee",
  extends: Person,
  properties: {
    id: p.integer().primary(),
    badge: () => p.oneToOne(Badge).owner().eager(),
  },
});
```

### Issue

Fetching an `Employee` no longer populates the eager `badge` relation:

```TypeScript
const found = await em.findOneOrFail(Employee, { id: 1 }, { populate: ["*"] });

found.badge; // null — should be a Badge instance
```

The debug log reveals the cause. Without the filter the second query (loading `Badge`) produces clean left joins for the inverse back-references:

```sql
-- Without filter (filters: false) — badge IS populated ✓
select `b0`.*,
  `p2`.`id` as `p1__id`, `p2`.`name` as `p1__name`, `p2`.`deleted_at` as `p1__deleted_at`,
  `p1`.`badge_id` as `p1__badge_id`,
  `p4`.`id` as `p3__id`, `p4`.`name` as `p3__name`, `p4`.`deleted_at` as `p3__deleted_at`,
  `p3`.`temporary_badge_id` as `p3__temporary_badge_id`
from `badge` as `b0`
left join (`person_employee` as `p1` inner join `person` as `p2` on `p1`.`id` = `p2`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p1`.`badge_id`
left join (`person_contractor` as `p3` inner join `person` as `p4` on `p3`.`id` = `p4`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p3`.`temporary_badge_id`
where `b0`.`id` in (1)
```

With the filter active, MikroORM emits **duplicate JOINs** for the same two tables — one filtered pair (`p1`/`p3`, with `deleted_at is null` on the JOIN condition) and one unfiltered pair (`p5`/`p7`):

```sql
-- With filter (default: true) — badge is NOT populated ✗
select `b0`.*,
  `p2`.`id` as `p1__id`, `p2`.`name` as `p1__name`, `p2`.`deleted_at` as `p1__deleted_at`,
  `p1`.`badge_id` as `p1__badge_id`,
  `p4`.`id` as `p3__id`, `p4`.`name` as `p3__name`, `p4`.`deleted_at` as `p3__deleted_at`,
  `p3`.`temporary_badge_id` as `p3__temporary_badge_id`,
  `p6`.`id` as `p5__id`,   -- duplicate, unfiltered — only selects id
  `p8`.`id` as `p7__id`    -- duplicate, unfiltered — only selects id
from `badge` as `b0`
left join (`person_employee` as `p1` inner join `person` as `p2` on `p1`.`id` = `p2`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p1`.`badge_id` and `p2`.`deleted_at` is null        -- filtered
left join (`person_contractor` as `p3` inner join `person` as `p4` on `p3`.`id` = `p4`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p3`.`temporary_badge_id` and `p4`.`deleted_at` is null  -- filtered
left join (`person_employee` as `p5` inner join `person` as `p6` on `p5`.`id` = `p6`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p5`.`badge_id`                                       -- duplicate, unfiltered
left join (`person_contractor` as `p7` inner join `person` as `p8` on `p7`.`id` = `p8`.`id`)
  on `b0`.`id` = `p7`.`temporary_badge_id`                             -- duplicate, unfiltered
where `b0`.`id` in (1)
```

The unfiltered duplicate joins (`p5`/`p7`) select only `id` — no FK columns. They appear to be used by MikroORM's hydration for relationship detection, and cause MikroORM to hydrate the `badge` property on `Employee` as `null`.

### Expectation

The `badge` relation should be populated regardless of whether a filter is applied to the base TPT entity. The two queries should be identical except for the `deleted_at is null` condition on the first query's `WHERE` clause.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/stoneLeaf/mikro-orm-v7-repros/tree/tpt-base-filter-breaks-eager-onetoone-population

@mikro-orm/postgresql

items.title: MikroORM 7 getKysely typing omits relation-backed FK columns for decorator class entities (but works with defineEntity)
items.body:
### Describe the bug

### Summary
When using getKysely with decorator-based class entities, relation-backed foreign key columns are missing from inferred Kysely table types.

The same model works with defineEntity because that path preserves richer compile-time property metadata for relation fields.

### Minimal Repro

1. Define entities with decorators:

```typescript
import { Entity, PrimaryKey, Property, ManyToOne } from "@mikro-orm/decorators/legacy";
import { EntityName, UuidType, type Rel } from "@mikro-orm/postgresql";

@Entity()
class Author {
  [EntityName]?: "Author";
  @PrimaryKey({ type: UuidType }) id!: string;
  @Property() name!: string;
}

@Entity()
class Book {
  [EntityName]?: "Book";
  @PrimaryKey({ type: UuidType }) id!: string;
  @Property() title!: string;
  @ManyToOne(() => Author) author!: Rel<Author>;
}

const db = orm.em.getKysely();

db.selectFrom("book").select("book.title");      // typed OK
db.selectFrom("book").select("book.author");     // relation not available
db.selectFrom("book").select("book.author_id");  // expected FK column not inferred
```

2. Define equivalent model with defineEntity and observe FK inference is available.

### Expected
Decorator class entities also infer relation-backed FK columns (for example author_id)

### Actual
Decorator path infers scalar class properties only; relation properties and relation-backed FK columns are absent.

### Root Cause (type flow, decorator path)
Current getKysely typing is effectively an intersection of two sources:

- Schema-derived path
- Class fallback path

In simplified form:
```typescript
Kysely<
  InferKyselyDB<EntitiesFromManager<this>, TOptions>
  &
  InferClassEntityDB<AllEntitiesFromManager<this>, TOptions>
>
```
For decorator classes, the relevant fallback is:

    InferClassEntityDB -> ClassEntityColumns -> IsClassEntityColumn

And IsClassEntityColumn is scalar-gated:
```typescript
type IsClassEntityColumn<K, V> =
  K extends symbol ? never : NonNullable<V> extends Scalar ? K : never;
```

So relation properties like author: Rel<Author> are excluded at type level, which explains why only scalar fields appear.

### Why defineEntity works
The defineEntity path carries property-builder metadata in EntitySchemaWithMeta properties, including relation kind information. The schema inference path can then derive FK column names and key types (for example author_id) from that metadata.

In other words:
- defineEntity path: metadata-rich, relation-aware inference
- decorator class fallback path: scalar-only class-property filter

### Versions
- @mikro-orm/core: 7.0.4
- @mikro-orm/decorators: 7.0.4
- @mikro-orm/postgresql: 7.0.4
- kysely: 0.28.14

items.title: Polymorphic relation issue with default filters
Honour the returning property differently, or allow use of a forceReturning property
items.body:
We recently updated to mikro-orm v6.6.8 and have noticed a difference in how the returning clause is generated in create queries. Previously, our id fields were being returned having been assigned server-side. We would provide a null id and a database trigger would assign an appropriate value, and mikro-orm would successfully pick this value up.

Examining the latest code for entity creation, I see:

```
const returningProps = meta.props
    .filter(prop => prop.persist !== false && prop.defaultRaw || prop.autoincrement || prop.generated)
    .filter(prop => !(prop.name in data[0]) || core_1.Utils.isRawSql(data[0][prop.name]));
```
It's clear that if the prop name is supplied in the first data row, it will be excluded from the returning props. I presume this is because it is assumed that if the data is provided, there's no need to return it?

Ideally, I'd like for the returning option to be honoured, so that if it is set, a field will always be added to the returning clause. Alternatively, if this would be a problem elsewhere in the library, could a forceReturn property be added that ensures that a specific field is always included in the returning clause?

For a simple test, I changed the above to:
```
            const returningProps = meta.props
                .filter(prop => prop.persist !== false && prop.defaultRaw || prop.autoincrement || prop.generated || prop.returning)
                .filter(prop => prop.returning || !(prop.name in data[0]) || core_1.Utils.isRawSql(data[0][prop.name]));
```

And the fields I set to returning were correctly processed. I am unsure whether this will cause an issue elsewhere, though.

Looking at the current source, it seems as though returning is not always considered when constructing the returning clause. Is this intentional?
